hints: Focus on what increasing concentration actually changes about the particles in the same volume.
More propanone molecules crowded into the same volume means the particles are closer together and meet $\text{I}_2$ more often.
Connect collision frequency to rate, remembering that energy per particle and the fraction that can react stay the same.
walkthrough:
**Picture what higher concentration means**

Think simply. Same volume, but more $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ particles squeezed in. They are closer together, not further apart.

$$\text{higher concentration} = \text{more particles per unit volume}$$

**Apply collision theory**

For a reaction to happen, $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ particles must collide. More particles in the same space means more collisions every second.

$$\text{rate} \propto \text{collision frequency}$$

**Check what does not change**

Concentration does not give particles more energy, and it does not lower the activation energy. So the proportion of collisions that are successful stays the same, there are just more of them, so initial rate increases.

options.A: Incorrect. The proportion or fraction of successful collisions depends on activation energy and temperature, not concentration. Concentration increases the total number of collisions, not the percentage that have enough energy.
options.B: Incorrect and opposite to the truth. At higher concentration there are more particles in the same volume, so particles are closer together, not further apart.
options.C: Incorrect. Average energy of particles depends on temperature, not concentration. Adding more propanone does not make each particle move faster or have more kinetic energy.
options.D: Correct. With more $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ particles in the same total volume, $\text{I}_2$ and propanone meet more often. More collisions per second means more successful collisions per second, so the initial rate increases.
